section.title: Save Me, O God
section.sectionRationale: One of the great passion psalms of the Old Testament, quoted more often in the New Testament than almost any other psalm, this lament moves from David sinking in miry, overwhelming waters through undeserved reproach for God's sake, gall and vinegar offered for comfort, a sustained plea that God's justice fall on unrepentant enemies, and finally to a vow of praise and hope for Zion's restoration, its details fulfilled directly in Christ's zeal, thirst, and abandonment at the cross.
section.thesis: David's cry from waters up to his neck, borne out of undeserved reproach endured for God's own sake, is taken up by the New Testament as the very voice of Christ, whose zeal for His Father's house, whose thirst answered with vinegar, and whose betrayer's judgment are each traced to this psalm, showing that even its hardest verses, the plea for God's justice on the unrepentant, are honest, Spirit-given prayer entrusting vengeance to God rather than seizing it for oneself.
section.frameNote: Seven movements: the cry from overwhelming waters and miry depths, verses 1-6; undeserved reproach endured for God's sake, becoming a stranger even to family, verses 7-12; a renewed plea for rescue from the mire, verses 13-18; insults, gall, and vinegar as the psalm's climax of undeserved suffering, verses 19-21; the sustained imprecation praying God's justice on the unrepentant, verses 22-28; a vow of praise that pleases God more than sacrifice, verses 29-33; and the closing hope that heaven, earth, and Zion's rebuilt cities would praise Him, verses 34-36.

units.label: Save me, O God
units.note: the cry from overwhelming waters and miry depths

verses.text: Save me, O God, for the waters are up to my neck.
I have sunk into the miry depths, where there is no footing; I have drifted into deep waters, where the flood engulfs me.
I am weary from my crying; my throat is parched. My eyes fail, looking for my God.
Those who hate me without cause outnumber the hairs of my head; many are those who would destroy me, my enemies for no reason. Though I did not steal, I must repay.
You know my folly, O God, and my guilt is not hidden from You.
May those who hope in You not be ashamed through me, O Lord GOD of Hosts; may those who seek You not be dishonored through me, O God of Israel.

units.label: Zeal for Your house has consumed me
units.note: undeserved reproach, a stranger even to family

verses.text: For I have endured scorn for Your sake, and shame has covered my face.
I have become a stranger to my brothers and a foreigner to my mother's sons,
because {{qinah|zeal}} for Your house has consumed me, and the insults of those who insult You have fallen on me.
I wept and fasted, but it brought me reproach.
I made sackcloth my clothing, and I was sport to them.
Those who sit at the gate mock me, and I am the song of drunkards.
But my prayer to You, O Lord, is for a time of favor. In Your abundant loving devotion, O God, answer me with Your sure salvation.
Rescue me from the mire and do not let me sink; deliver me from my foes and out of the deep waters.
Do not let the floods engulf me or the depths swallow me up; let not the Pit close its mouth over me.
Answer me, O Lord, for Your loving devotion is good; turn to me in keeping with Your great compassion.
Hide not Your face from Your servant, for I am in distress. Answer me quickly!
Draw near to my soul and redeem me; ransom me because of my foes.

units.label: They gave me gall and vinegar

verses.text: You know my reproach, my shame and disgrace. All my adversaries are before You.
Insults have broken my heart, and I am in despair. I looked for sympathy, but there was none, for comforters, but I found no one.
They poisoned my food with {{rosh|gall}} and gave me vinegar to quench my thirst.

units.label: Pour out Your wrath upon them
units.note: the sustained plea for God's justice on the unrepentant

verses.text: May their table become a snare; may it be a retribution and a trap.
May their eyes be darkened so they cannot see, and their backs be bent forever.
Pour out Your wrath upon them, and let Your burning anger overtake them.
May their place be deserted; let there be no one to dwell in their tents.
For they persecute the one You struck and recount the pain of those You wounded.
Add iniquity to their iniquity; let them not share in Your righteousness.
May they be blotted out of the Book of Life and not listed with the righteous.

units.label: I will praise God's name in song
units.note: a vow of praise that pleases God more than sacrifice

verses.text: But I am in pain and distress; let Your salvation protect me, O God.
I will praise God's name in song and exalt Him with thanksgiving.
And this will please the Lord more than an ox, more than a bull with horns and hooves.
The humble will see and rejoice. You who seek God, let your hearts be revived!
For the Lord listens to the needy and does not despise His captive people.

units.label: Let heaven and earth praise Him
units.note: the closing hope for Zion's restoration

verses.text: Let heaven and earth praise Him, the seas and everything that moves in them.
For God will save Zion and rebuild the cities of Judah, that they may dwell there and possess it.
The descendants of His servants will inherit it, and those who love His name will settle in it.

qinah.gloss: Zeal, jealous devotion, an intense, consuming passion for God's honor. John's Gospel applies this very word directly to Jesus when He cleansed the temple, John 2:17, seeing His action as the fulfillment of this psalm's zeal that 'consumed' the psalmist.

rosh.gloss: Gall, a bitter, poisonous herb, mixed here with food as an act of cruelty toward the sufferer. Together with the vinegar offered for thirst, this detail is fulfilled precisely at the cross, where Jesus was offered wine mixed with gall and, later, sour wine, Matthew 27:34, 48.

basic.context: David cries out from what feels like drowning, waters up to his neck, hated without cause, and estranged even from his own family because of his zeal for God's house. He is mocked, given gall and vinegar instead of comfort, and prays urgently both for his own rescue and for God's justice on his unrepentant enemies.
basic.hermeneutics: This psalm is quoted more often in the New Testament than almost any other, applied directly to Christ's zeal, His thirst on the cross, and the judgment on His betrayer. Its imprecations are not personal vengeance but a Spirit-inspired prayer entrusting justice to God alone.
basic.originalLanguages: David's qinah, zeal, for God's house consumes him, verse 9, the very word John applies to Jesus cleansing the temple, John 2:17. And his enemies give him rosh, gall, mixed with his food, verse 21, fulfilled precisely at the cross, Matthew 27:34.
basic.typology: Nearly every major section of this psalm is applied to Christ in the New Testament, His zeal for the temple, John 2:17, being hated without cause, John 15:25, His thirst answered with gall and vinegar, Matthew 27:34, 48, and the imprecation against His betrayer's household, applied to Judas in Acts 1:20.
basic.christ: This is one of the clearest messianic psalms in the Psalter. Jesus' disciples remembered 'zeal for Your house will consume Me' when He cleansed the temple, John 2:17. Jesus quoted verse 4 of Himself, 'they hated Me without a cause,' John 15:25. He fulfilled verse 21 literally on the cross, given sour wine, John 19:28-30. And Peter applies the imprecation of verse 25 directly to Judas Iscariot's fate, Acts 1:20.
basic.god: God is shown as the one who hears the cry of the drowning and the falsely accused, who allows His anointed to suffer reproach for His own sake, and whose coming justice on the unrepentant, prayed for honestly here, is neither denied nor apologized for anywhere in Scripture, but is entrusted entirely to Him rather than seized by human hands.
basic.crossReferences: John 2:17 applies this psalm's zeal for God's house directly to Jesus cleansing the temple. Matthew 27:34, 48 fulfill the gall and vinegar offered to Jesus on the cross. Romans 11:9-10 and Acts 1:20 apply this psalm's imprecations to the judgment on unbelieving Israel and on Judas respectively.
basic.oneStory: David's undeserved suffering for God's sake, his thirst answered with gall and vinegar, and his plea that God's justice fall on the unrepentant, all find their fulfillment in Christ, whose zeal, thirst, and betrayal this psalm precisely anticipates, and whose cross absorbs the very reproach David describes so that all who trust Him might finally, fully be saved.

context.literary:
Psalm 69 is carefully built, and it is easy to miss the craft under the pain. The heading gives the tune as 'Lilies,' the same heading as Psalm 45 and Psalm 80, which tells us that a cry this dark was sung to a known melody in the temple. The poem breaks into panels. Verses 1 to 4 describe drowning and the multitude of enemies. Verses 5 to 12 move from the private sense of sin to the public cost of devotion, 'for Your sake,' and 'for Your house.' Verses 13 to 18 are the turn, marked by the word 'But' in verse 13, where the cry becomes a prayer to a God of loving devotion. Verses 19 to 21 return to the suffering with a sharper point, reproach, loneliness, gall and vinegar. Verses 22 to 28 are the long imprecation. And verses 29 to 36 arrive, again after a 'But,' at praise and a hope for Zion.

Two words, 'But,' in verses 13 and 29, mark the psalm's turns. Both come directly after a description of pain, and both shift from 'they' to 'I' and from 'I' to 'You.' The psalm does not explain pain away, and it does not leave its speaker in the mud. Its movement is from the water up to the ground, and the ground is the praise of verses 30 to 33.

The water imagery frames the first half. The waters come 'up to my neck' in verse 1, and the psalmist prays in verses 14 and 15 that he would not sink, that the floods would not engulf him, and that the Pit would not close its mouth over him. It is a chiastic echo: what threatened in verse 1 is what he asks to be delivered from in verse 15. And the prayer of verse 13 has its own care. 'A time of favor' sits beside 'abundant loving devotion' and 'sure salvation,' three words that put the weight on God's character instead of the psalmist's merit.

A further pattern is the repetition of 'You know.' The psalmist says 'You know my folly' in verse 5 and 'You know my reproach' in verse 19. The first is about his sin and the second about his shame, and in both cases he appeals to a God who sees everything and is not deceived. The psalm is a petition to a God who knows more than the speaker can say.
context.historical:
The heading calls the psalm Davidic, and the life of David gives it plenty of occasions: his brothers' scorn at the battle with Goliath, 1 Samuel 17:28, Saul's years of pursuit, the rebellion of Absalom, and the curses of Shimei, 2 Samuel 16:5-8. None of these is named in the psalm, and the lack of a named occasion has let the psalm be sung by many sufferers. Verses 35 and 36 speak of God saving Zion and rebuilding the cities of Judah, which has led some readers to think that the last lines were added, or the whole psalm adapted, in the time of the exile. Others see the lines as David's own prophetic hope, or as a petition that assumes Zion and Judah in danger.

The details fit the world of the gate and the temple. 'Those who sit at the gate' in verse 12 are the elders and idlers who held the public space of the city, where legal business and gossip were both conducted, Ruth 4:1-2. A man mocked there is shamed in the place where his reputation is made. 'The song of drunkards' in the same verse names the taunt-songs that might be made about a person at a feast. Sackcloth and fasting in verses 10 and 11 were the normal signs of mourning and penitence, and the psalm describes how the act of humility was itself turned into mockery.

Verse 4, 'Though I did not steal, I must repay,' suggests a situation where he is made to pay for what he did not take, a kind of false judgment. Verse 8, where the psalmist is 'a stranger to my brothers' and 'a foreigner to my mother's sons,' is especially painful in a culture where family was the centre of identity and protection, Verse 9's 'zeal for Your house' could be David's concern for the ark and the place of worship, 2 Samuel 7:2 and Psalm 132:1-5. The psalm never tells us the story, and the point of its silence is that every reader can put their own in.
context.canonical:
Psalm 69 is one of the most quoted psalms in the New Testament, ranking beside Psalm 22 and Psalm 110. It belongs to a family of laments in which an innocent sufferer speaks, Psalms 22, 35, 38, 40, 88 and 109. Its phrase 'hate me without cause' has a twin in Psalm 35:19, and its waters and mire recall Psalm 40:2 and Psalm 42:7. The closing turn to Zion's rebuilding ties it to the exile psalms, and the placing of it after Psalm 68's shout of triumph is a striking contrast: the victory hymn is followed by the cup of suffering.

The New Testament quotes it in at least five places. John 2:17 gives the disciples remembering verse 9a at the cleansing of the temple. John 15:25 uses verse 4 to explain why Jesus was hated, 'in their Law,' which shows that 'the Law' there means Scripture as a whole. Romans 15:3 quotes the second half of verse 9, 'The insults of those who insult You have fallen on Me,' as the pattern of Christ bearing others' reproach. Romans 11:9-10 uses verses 22 and 23 about Israel's hardening, and Acts 1:20 applies verse 25 to Judas, together with Psalm 109:8. The gall and vinegar of verse 21 lie behind the scene at the cross, Matthew 27:34, 48 and John 19:28-29.

Other New Testament passages draw on the psalm less directly. Mark 3:21 and John 7:5 record the unbelief of Jesus' own family, which matches verse 8. The appeal in verse 13 to 'a time of favor' meets Isaiah 49:8, and Paul says 'now is the time of favor' in 2 Corinthians 6:2. The 'Book of Life' of verse 28 connects to Exodus 32:32-33, Daniel 12:1, Philippians 4:3 and Revelation 3:5 and 20:15. And the picture of heaven and earth praising in verse 34 leads to the creation's songs in Revelation 5:13.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist means to show that honest prayer can hold sorrow, shame, confession and anger together. It does not sanitise the experience. The reader meets a man who is sinking, who is hated for no reason, and whose devotion to God's house has cost him his family. Yet he speaks throughout to God, and he never turns to revenge, but hands his enemies over to divine judgment. A congregation that sang it was being taught how to bring the worst to God, and how to hope in the same breath.

The psalm also makes a point about the community. In verse 6 the speaker prays that those who hope in God will 'not be ashamed through me.' He knows that his fate is bound up with the faith of others, and that if the righteous man is abandoned, the godly will be discouraged. So the psalm is not about one man's misery. It is about what a public display of God's faithfulness or apparent failure would mean to everyone who waits for Him. The final section gives the answer: the humble will 'see and rejoice,' verse 32, because God has listened.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes a particular sufferer's experience and his prayer. It does not tell anyone to expect the same sufferings, or to pray the same curses. The imprecations of verses 22 to 28 are words put in the mouth of a king or a righteous sufferer who is asking God, not himself, to judge. They describe a prayer; they do not prescribe a personal campaign of hatred. Jesus says to love enemies and pray for those who persecute, Matthew 5:44, and Jesus Himself prayed for His executioners, Luke 23:34.

What carries forward is the pattern of taking everything to God, including the ugly feelings, and leaving vengeance with Him, Romans 12:19. The psalm also prescribes humility in verse 5, where the sufferer does not claim to be spotless, and it gives believers a script for lament that ends in praise. Its use in the New Testament for Christ gives a further lesson: when we read the psalm we are reading the prayer of the Righteous One, and our own suffering is joined to His, 1 Peter 2:21-23.

debates.question: How can Jesus be the speaker of the psalm when verse 5 confesses 'my folly' and 'my guilt'?

views.label: David speaks, and the psalm is fulfilled in Christ by pattern
views.case: Verse 5 is David's honest confession, and the New Testament uses the psalm about Christ in the parts that fit Him: zeal, hatred without cause, thirst, betrayal. It does not quote verse 5 of Christ. On this view the psalm is a typical psalm, a righteous sufferer's prayer, in which the pattern, not every line, is fulfilled in Jesus.

views.label: Christ speaks as the one who bears our folly
views.case: Psalm 40:12, in which 'my sins have overtaken me,' is put into Christ's mouth in Hebrews 10:5-7 in a nearby verse, and Paul says God made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, 2 Corinthians 5:21. Some therefore hear verse 5 as Christ speaking about the guilt He took on, not guilt of His own. The folly is ours, and He owns it in our place.

views.label: The confession is of general sinfulness, not of the accusations
views.case: Verse 4 says the charge he must answer, theft, is false, and verse 5 says God knows his real folly. The speaker is saying that God alone knows the truth about him and will judge rightly, and that a man can be innocent of the charge while guilty before God in other ways. This leaves space for David's own confession and for Christ's fulfilment by contrast.

debates.bearing: The New Testament does not press verse 5 on Jesus, and careful readers need not. The pattern of the righteous sufferer is fulfilled in Him, and the plea of verse 5 can be read as David's own honest word, while the wider story of Christ bearing our guilt stands on other texts such as Isaiah 53:4-6.

debates.question: How should Christians pray or read the curses of verses 22 to 28?

views.label: Inspired declarations of judgment
views.case: Paul uses verses 22 and 23 for Israel's hardening, Romans 11:9-10, and Peter uses verse 25 for Judas, Acts 1:20. The New Testament treats them as true statements of God's justice on those who reject His Anointed, not as petty vengeance.

views.label: The honest voice of a sufferer handing judgment to God
views.case: The curses are the cry of a man who will not take revenge himself but asks God to act. They model the practice of laying injustice before God, and they should be read along with the gospel's fuller revelation that the final judgment belongs to Christ, John 5:22, and that the church's weapons are not of this world.

views.label: A voice the gospel both hears and reshapes
views.case: Many teachers say the psalm teaches that evil is to be taken seriously and that God's justice is not optional, while Jesus' teaching on love of enemies and His prayer on the cross show how those with power are to treat their persecutors now, Luke 23:34 and Romans 12:14-21.

debates.bearing: All three views agree that the believer does not take vengeance. The psalm's curses are given to God, and in Christ the cup of wrath is drunk by the innocent, so the way of the church toward enemies is prayer and mercy while the last word on judgment is left with the Lord.

study.originalLanguages:
Start with the water in verse 1. The BSB reads 'the waters are up to my neck,' and the Hebrew is nephesh, which usually means 'life' or 'soul' and here likely means the throat. The BSB does not flag it, but the word is telling: the water has reached the place where breath and life are. Jonah's prayer has the same thought, with the waters closing in up to the point of life itself, Jonah 2:5. The psalmist feels the danger at the very seat of life. The 'miry depths' and the 'Pit' in verses 2 and 15 belong to the language of Sheol, the place of the dead, and the psalm is asking for rescue from something close to death.

Second, verse 9 has the word for 'zeal,' qin'ah, which comes from a root for passion or jealousy and is used of God's own jealous love, Exodus 20:5, and of Phinehas' zeal, Numbers 25:11. The verb 'consumed' is literally 'eaten,' akhal, so that zeal has eaten him as a fire eats what it burns. John 2:17 uses a future verb, 'will consume Me,' in Greek, which fits the disciples' reading of what was about to happen to Jesus as a result of the temple cleansing. The second half of verse 9 speaks of 'the insults of those who insult You,' a construction where the object of the insult is God and the one who bears it is the worshiper. Paul quotes this in Romans 15:3.

Third, in verse 11 the word rendered 'sport' is mashal, which elsewhere means a proverb or a byword. To become a mashal is to become a figure of speech, a thing people point to and say 'may you be like him.' It is the same word used in Deuteronomy 28:37, where exile is said to make Israel a byword. The psalmist has been turned into a proverb of shame. In verse 12 the 'song of drunkards' uses a different word for music, neginah, the stringed song, and puts his misery into a drinking tune.

Fourth, the prayer of verse 18 uses two of the great verbs of redemption together: 'redeem me,' ga'al, and 'ransom me,' padah. The first is the word for the kinsman-redeemer who takes up the cause of a relative, as Boaz does in Ruth 3:12-13. The second is the language of paying a price to free someone, as in Exodus 13:13. The psalmist is asking God to play the part of the next of kin who stands with him when his real kin have cast him off, verse 8. In verse 13 the prayer rests on 'the truth of Your salvation,' which the BSB renders 'sure salvation,' the Hebrew having emet, reliability, at its centre.

Fifth, the gall of verse 21. The Hebrew rosh names a bitter or poisonous plant, and Deuteronomy 29:18 and 32:32 use the same word of a bitter, poisonous root. The psalm says 'they poisoned my food with gall and gave me vinegar to quench my thirst,' and the pair, gall for food and vinegar for thirst, is what the Gospels describe. The word 'vinegar,' chomets, is sour wine, the drink of labourers, as in Ruth 2:14. Finally, the 'Book of Life' in verse 28 is literally 'the book of the living.' To be blotted out is the verb used when Moses said 'blot me out of the book that You have written,' Exodus 32:32, and it is one of the few places where the Old Testament speaks of a register of those who belong to God. In verse 27, 'add iniquity to their iniquity' uses a word, avon, that can mean either guilt or its punishment, so the line can be read as a prayer that they be given the full weight of their own guilt.

typology.type: The sufferer zealous for God's house, verses 7 to 9
typology.fulfillment: David bore scorn because zeal for God's house consumed him, and family turned from him. The disciples saw this pattern when Jesus drove the traders from the temple and remembered the verse, John 2:13-17, and John records that His brothers did not believe in Him, John 7:5. Paul cites verse 9b for Christ's whole life of bearing reproach for others, Romans 15:3. The escalation is that Jesus is the true dwelling of God, John 2:19-21, and His zeal leads to the cross. The type falls short in that David's zeal was mixed with folly, verse 5, while Christ's was sinless.

David's enemies were many and without reason, and the psalm is among the texts Jesus meant when He said 'they hated Me without a cause,' John 15:25. The correspondence is that an innocent man is opposed by those who should have welcomed him. In Christ it is the religious leaders and then the powers of the age who hate the one who did them only good, John 10:32 and Luke 23:13-25. The escalation is that His rejection is the means by which the world's guilt is carried, 1 Peter 2:23-24. The type falls short in that David could only ask for justice, while Christ's death became the atonement.

The psalmist looked for comfort and was given poison and sour wine. At the cross Jesus was offered wine mixed with gall and refused it, Matthew 27:34, and later, knowing that all was finished, He said 'I am thirsty' and was given sour wine, John 19:28-30. The Gospels tell the story in the psalm's own words. The escalation is that the thirst was the thirst of the one who bore God's judgment, and the cup He drank was the cup of wrath, Mark 14:36. The type falls short since David's thirst was a figure of speech in a prayer, while Christ's was literal and redemptive.

The psalm asks that the dwelling of the wicked be deserted, and Peter applies it to Judas, who betrayed the Lord and died in a field he had bought with the price of betrayal, Acts 1:16-20. The correspondence is that one who joined the circle of the Anointed and then turned against Him falls under judgment. The place left empty is filled, for another is chosen to take his office, Acts 1:21-26. The type falls short in that the psalm names no person, and Peter's use is an apostolic application rather than an original prediction of one man.

study.christ:
The New Testament takes this psalm as the prayer of the righteous sufferer and finds Jesus in it from the beginning of His ministry to His death. Start with the zeal of verse 9. When He drove out the sellers from the temple the disciples remembered 'Zeal for Your house will consume Me,' John 2:17, and they saw in that act the pattern of His whole life. Paul carries the second half of the verse further: Christ 'did not please Himself' but bore the insults of those who insulted God, Romans 15:3. The reproach of verse 9b is the insult hurled at God by a world in revolt, and the Son took it in His own body.

The estrangement of verse 8 is also His. John writes that even His brothers did not believe in Him, John 7:5, and Mark says His family set out to take charge of Him, for people were saying 'He is out of His mind,' Mark 3:21. The hatred 'without cause' of verse 4 is His, since He cites it, John 15:25. The reproach, the mocking at the gate and the song of drunkards find their counterpart in the soldiers' mockery, the crowds' jeers and the chief priests' taunts, Matthew 27:27-44. The sense of looking for comforters and finding no one, verse 20, is His in Gethsemane when His disciples slept, Matthew 26:40, and on the cross when He was forsaken, Matthew 27:46.

Then there is the cross itself. The gall and the vinegar, verse 21, are given at the place and the hour, Matthew 27:34 and 48, and John says that Jesus said 'I am thirsty' in order that Scripture might be fulfilled, John 19:28-30. The deep waters of verses 1 and 2 are the depths He entered for us, and Jesus spoke of His death as a baptism and a cup, Luke 12:50 and Mark 10:38-39. The man who says 'the waters are up to my neck' is the Lord who went down into them for the sake of others, and the psalm's prayer 'rescue me from the mire' is answered in His resurrection, Acts 2:24.

The psalm also points to what Christ does with the curse. The enemies in verses 22 to 28 are warned, and Peter applies verse 25 to Judas, while Paul applies verses 22 and 23 to a hardened Israel, Romans 11:7-10. But Paul goes on in the same chapter to say that their hardening is not final, Romans 11:11-12, 25-26, and Jesus on the cross prays for forgiveness for His persecutors, Luke 23:34. So the same Lord who fulfils the lament also carries its hardest lines, and in Him both justice and mercy are honoured.

A caution. The psalm does not call itself a prophecy, and verse 5, with its 'my folly,' is David's. The better way to put it is that Jesus is the righteous sufferer of the psalm in whom its pattern finds its full and sinless expression, and that He bears, in His person, the reproach, the thirst and the desertion it describes. The last verses, in which the humble see and rejoice, God saves Zion and the descendants of His servants inherit it, verses 32 to 36, are the hope that He secures by His resurrection and that Revelation 21:3 and 22:3-5 describe.
study.god:
Psalm 69 presents a God who knows. The refrain 'You know my folly,' verse 5, and 'You know my reproach,' verse 19, are not a complaint that God has failed to notice but an appeal to a God who misses nothing. The psalmist's whole strategy rests on the conviction that the judge sees the truth about both his sin and his innocence. This is a strong teaching about the omniscience of God, and it is comforting to the falsely accused and sobering for the guilty. Elsewhere Psalm 139:1-4 and Hebrews 4:13 say the same.

It also presents a God who can be spoken to honestly. The psalm contains words of despair, 'I am in despair,' verse 20, charges of being let down, 'my eyes fail, looking for my God,' verse 3, and a fierce call for judgment. God is not offended by any of it. The canon has made room for this prayer and set it to music, which tells us something about the God who receives it. He is not fragile, and He is not shocked by the cry of a man in the mud.

The psalm places the grounds of the plea in God's character: 'Your abundant loving devotion,' 'Your sure salvation,' 'Your great compassion,' verses 13 and 16. The same pairing of steadfast love and compassion appears in God's name at Sinai, Exodus 34:6, and the psalmist draws on it as a right earned by promise, not by merit. Verse 16's 'Your loving devotion is good' is a small, bold sentence: the goodness of God's covenant love is the ground of the prayer.

The psalm balances mercy and justice. God is the one who draws near to redeem, verse 18, and the one who pours out wrath on those who persist in evil, verse 24. The two are not in conflict, for the same covenant faithfulness that rescues the needy condemns those who oppress them. The last verses show where that leads: God 'listens to the needy and does not despise His captive people,' verse 33, and He will 'save Zion and rebuild the cities of Judah,' verse 35. He is a God who restores what has been ruined.

For worship, this gives three things. It gives permission to pray with everything, with the anger, the shame and the confession in the same prayer. It gives a ground, the character of God and not the record of the one who prays. And it gives an ending: the psalm moves toward a song that 'will please the LORD more than an ox,' verse 31, and so teaches that the praise of a rescued heart is worth more to God than all the sacrifices of the altar.

crossReferences.note: The disciples remember 'Zeal for Your house will consume Me' as Jesus clears the temple. They saw in His passion for God's house the same fire that burned in David, and saw also that it would cost Him His life.

Jesus says the word written in their Law, 'They hated Me without a cause,' is fulfilled in the world's hatred of Him. It gives Psalm 69:4 a place in His own account of why He was rejected, and shows that 'Law' here means the whole of Scripture.

'The insults of those who insult You have fallen on Me.' Paul uses the second half of Psalm 69:9 to show that Christ did not please Himself but bore the reproach due to others, and he asks the strong to bear with the weak in the same way.

Jesus is offered wine mixed with gall, and after tasting it He refuses to drink. It is the nearest New Testament match to Psalm 69:21, and the Gospel tells the scene in the psalm's own terms, with the poisonous bitterness of the plant and the sour drink.

Jesus says 'I am thirsty' so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, and is given sour wine. It is the second half of Psalm 69:21, and it joins the thirst of the suffering man to the last word of the cross, 'It is finished.'

Peter applies 'May their place be deserted' to Judas, together with Psalm 109:8 about another taking his office. It shows the apostolic method of reading a psalm of the righteous sufferer as applying to the betrayer of the Anointed.

Paul quotes Psalm 69:22 and 23, 'Let their table become a snare,' about those of Israel who were hardened. He then says the hardening is not final, so the curse of the psalm is placed within a larger purpose of mercy.

The prophet describes waters closing over him to the soul and the deep surrounding him, in words like those of Psalm 69:1-2. Both texts picture the descent toward death as drowning, and in both the cry to God is answered.

Moses asks to be 'blot[ted] out of the book' that God has written if God will not forgive Israel. It uses the same verb and the same image of God's book as Psalm 69:28, and it shows how heavy the register of the living is.

'In the time of favor I will answer You.' The phrase 'time of favor' appears in Psalm 69:13, and Paul cites Isaiah's version in 2 Corinthians 6:2. Together they show that the psalmist's hope for God's moment of answer is a hope the gospel says has arrived.

'Do not let those who are wrongfully my enemies gloat over me; do not let those who hate me without cause wink their eyes.' It is a close parallel to Psalm 69:4, and shows that 'hatred without cause' belongs to a pattern of the righteous sufferer in the Psalter.

Christ suffered for us, leaving an example, and 'when they hurled insults at Him, He did not retaliate.' It shows how the church learned to read psalms like Psalm 69, as the suffering of the Righteous One in whose steps believers follow.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 69 sits in the story at the place where a righteous person suffers for God's sake in a world that does not welcome Him. It answers the question raised in Genesis 3 and 4, when the first righteous man, Abel, is killed by his brother. Why do the innocent suffer, and where is God? The psalm does not give a theory. It gives a prayer, in which the innocent sufferer keeps speaking to God and waits for Him to answer.

It also answers a question the Old Testament raises about the king. David was promised a house and an everlasting throne, 2 Samuel 7:12-16, and yet he is presented in the Psalter as a man rejected, hated and alone. The psalm shows that the road of the anointed leads through reproach. That is a hint that the Messiah will be a suffering king, and Isaiah 53 gives it full voice: despised and rejected, a man of sorrows.

What it sets up is the passion of Christ. The Gospels quote the psalm at the temple and at the cross, and the church after Pentecost uses it to make sense of Judas and of Israel's resistance. The waters of verse 1 are the deep the Lord entered, and the gall and vinegar are the marks of His rejection. But the psalm also sets up what comes after the cross, for verse 29 turns, after another 'But,' to salvation, praise and Zion, and the resurrection is the answer to the cry 'do not let me sink.' His suffering is the way through the water for many.

It ends in new creation. The psalm's last verses call heaven, earth and the seas to praise, 'for God will save Zion,' and promise that 'those who love His name will settle in it.' The Bible's last chapters show that promise kept. The Lamb who was slain is on the throne, His people dwell in the city, and 'there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain,' Revelation 21:4. The man who felt the water rise to his neck is no longer alone, and the city he hoped for has come.

sermon.title: Pour Out Your Indignation Upon Them
sermon.why: Piper works through Psalm 69 as one of the most extended imprecatory psalms, showing from its New Testament citations, as the words of David and as the words of Jesus, that its curses are not sinful personal vengeance but sober, Spirit-inspired approval of God's coming justice, and an incentive for believers today to forbear and forgive precisely because vengeance belongs to God.

quiz.q: What image describes David's distress in verses 1-2?

options.text: Waters up to his neck, sunk in miry depths with no footing.
options.note: This drowning imagery pictures overwhelming, inescapable crisis.

options.text: A dry and thirsty land with no water at all.
options.note: That specific image belongs to Psalm 63; this psalm's crisis is too much water, not too little.

options.text: A quiet, peaceful garden.
options.note: The imagery is one of overwhelming crisis, not peace.

options.text: A battlefield strewn with weapons.
options.note: The specific image given is drowning in water and mire, not a battlefield.

quiz.q: Why does David say he has become 'a stranger to my brothers,' verse 8?

options.text: Because zeal for God's house has consumed him.
options.note: His devotion to God's honor itself becomes the reason for his estrangement, later applied to Jesus in John 2:17.

options.text: Because he committed a specific crime against his family.
options.note: The text ties his alienation to zeal for God, not personal wrongdoing against his family.

options.text: Because he moved to a foreign country.
options.note: The estrangement described is relational and spiritual, not geographic relocation.

options.text: Because his family disagreed with his choice of career.
options.note: The specific reason given is religious zeal for God's house, not a career dispute.

quiz.q: What did David's enemies give him instead of comfort, in verse 21?

options.text: Gall for food and vinegar for his thirst.
options.note: This detail is fulfilled literally at the cross, Matthew 27:34, 48.

options.text: Bread and fresh water.
options.note: The verse describes cruelty, gall and vinegar, not kindness.

options.text: Silver and gold as a bribe.
options.note: The specific gift named is bitter food and sour drink, not money.

options.text: Fine wine and rich food.
options.note: The verse specifically names gall and vinegar, deliberately bitter and undesirable, not fine provisions.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament apply this psalm's zeal 'for Your house,' verse 9?

options.text: To Jesus cleansing the temple, His disciples remembering this very verse.
options.note: John 2:17 explicitly cites this psalm in connection with Jesus' action in the temple.

options.text: To the building of Herod's temple by human labor alone.
options.note: The New Testament connects this verse to Jesus' zeal, not merely to the temple's construction.

options.text: The New Testament never references this verse.
options.note: John 2:17 directly quotes this verse in connection with Jesus.

options.text: To the disciples' zeal in building the early church.
options.note: The specific New Testament application is to Jesus Himself, not the disciples' later ministry.

quiz.q: According to Piper's sermon on this psalm, how should Christians understand its imprecations, verses 22-28?

options.text: As sober, Spirit-inspired words of coming judgment entrusted to God, not sinful personal vengeance.
options.note: The New Testament quotes these very verses approvingly, applying them to God's judgment rather than treating them as sin to be corrected.

options.text: As sinful outbursts the New Testament corrects and disavows.
options.note: The New Testament instead quotes these verses approvingly, in Romans 11 and Acts 1, rather than disavowing them.

options.text: As commands for believers to personally carry out against their enemies today.
options.note: The psalm entrusts judgment to God; it does not instruct believers to execute vengeance personally.

options.text: As poetic exaggeration with no real theological meaning.
options.note: The New Testament treats these words as substantive, meaningful prophecy, not mere poetic exaggeration.

questions: David cries out from waters up to his neck, feeling like he is drowning in his circumstances. What situation right now feels overwhelming enough that you need to cry out to God the way David does here?

David's zeal for God's house made him a stranger even to his own family, and this very zeal is later fulfilled in Christ. Has devotion to God ever cost you a relationship or created distance with people close to you, and how do you process that cost?

David was given gall and vinegar instead of comfort, a detail fulfilled literally at the cross. How does knowing that Christ personally experienced undeserved cruelty change how you bring your own experiences of betrayal or mistreatment to Him?

The psalm's imprecations pray for God's justice rather than seizing revenge personally. Where do you need to hand over a desire for vengeance to God rather than either suppressing it or acting on it yourself?

The psalm ends with hope that heaven, earth, and Zion's rebuilt cities would praise God, verses 34-36. What present difficulty do you need to hold alongside this larger hope, that God's ultimate purpose is restoration and praise, not despair?

translationNotes.note: Those who hate me without cause is quoted by Jesus directly of Himself in John 15:25, applying David's undeserved hostility to His own experience.
Zeal renders qinah, consuming, jealous devotion for God's honor, the very word John's Gospel applies to Jesus cleansing the temple, John 2:17.
May their table become a snare is quoted by Paul in Romans 11:9-10 concerning God's judgment on unbelieving Israel in his own day.
May their place be deserted; let there be no one to dwell in their tents is applied by Peter directly to Judas Iscariot's betrayal and fate in Acts 1:20.
